doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

title: Oscar Peterson's gala remarks and the problem of jazz clones
summary: He defends Oscar Peterson's comments and argues that every great player found his own sound; Rowe asks if jazz education breeds clones.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: were a lot of critics and historians that I take issue with because they are not of the same mold like the Leonard Feathers or the Dan Morgensterns. They don’t have the same kind of humbleness and the same kind of commitment. Some woman came up to me the other day because she was very disturbed about what Oscar Peterson said at the gala the other day. And she asked me, “What do you think about that?” I said, “He was absolutely on the money.” She said, “What?” I said, “Yes, he was telling you the truth. I mean don’t you respect what he had to say?” He’s not a man — I worked with Oscar — Oscar’s not a man that takes things lightly. And he doesn’t make comments to be cavalier. When he says something check it out. Because there’s pearls of wisdom. And Oscar Peterson, excuse me. I mean if you can’t respect him and try to just don’t get an attitude and start thinking oh well he’s just bitter or this that and the other. People spend too much time trying to easily categorize or pigeon-hole people too quickly without taking the time to understand what are the conditions that has brought a human being to that particular level of whatever. Whether we’re talking about the frustration factor or even the satisfaction. Life is much more complex than some people would — but everybody’s looking for the quick fix. They want the instant on. And this whole thing about jazz education can’t be about a Swanson T.V. dinner. You know you get a Charlie Parker Omni book and learn a few Charlie Parker solos and look at me, I’m playing instant jazz. It’s not about that. That’s not the way you develop what we were saying before about learning these melodies. Getting inside of hearing your own sound. Yes we are all influenced by different people but I’m tired of hearing Coltrane clones. Find your own sound. That’s what’s so beautiful about when you go back and listen to these guys. I mean Lester Young was Lester Young. Stan Getz is Stan Getz. Zoot Sims is Zoot Sims. Hank Mobley is Hank Mobley. Sonny Stitt is Sonny Stitt. Dizzy Gillespie is Dizzy Gillespie. Miles Davis is Miles Davis. Fats Navarro. On and on and on. We can do that on all the instruments. And what makes them special is because they are themselves. And if you’re not trying to find your own identity I mean Ernest Hemingway is not trying to be William Shakespeare. Bach wasn’t — you know Mozart wasn’t trying to be Bach. Stravinsky was not trying to be Wagner. People in the arts, just like actors and actresses. And it’s true in all professions when we look at it. So it’s not something that’s just only in music or even in art. Gauguin and Rembrandt. Renoir. All these people are different. They found their thing that becomes them. Frank Lloyd Wright. I.M. Pei.

Have we kind of created a conflict then with jazz education is now a big business with publications and method books and all that. And this gathering here obviously is positive in some aspects for the music, but is it creating too many of the people you’re talking about that just are spinning out what the book says? © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-
